Aside from the indicated duel implication, I believe after examining the
metagame of the !Tor deck in the tournament, our group agreed with the
original poster. The deck's construction and particular choice of cards was
ineffective. Initial examination indicated a rather large crypt. This of
course was probably to be intended to be modified in the draft meaning that
you had to have luck on your side to get a decent vamp of relatively low
capacity to offset the large crypt required to vote. The bloated number of
vote cards in the deck indicated that the designer intended the deck to be
capable of passing it's votes. This did not seem the case with the number of
cheap vote available to all the pre release decks. The certain lack of
stealth was also incapacitating. As far as the combat goes, it is true that
when the deck did hit with a weapon, it hurt. If you didn't have a weapon or
a manouver, good luck. If one decided to change the strategy and forego the
vote angle, your choice of bleed cards was very small (though Propaganda
proved excellent that day). In the end, the players of the deck tended to be
the most frustrated as the offence of the deck was lacking and the combat
was easily countered. In it's credit, that deck had the most effective
defence. We gave it a very high speedbump rating with all the intercept,
counter and misdirection available to it.

This isn't related to the original topic you posed. The simple answer
is workload. After some level of playtesting, there is a diminsihing
return on "tweaking" decks to balance against one another, because it
is a near-total unknown as to the exact environment that the deck will
be played in. Possibilities include:

1) Four player, one of each BH clan, with no deck mods
2) Five player, mixed decks from BH and other expansions, no deck mods
3) #1, plus 3 booster draft
4) #2, plus 3 booster draft
5) #1, plus 3 booster sealed
6) #2, plus 3 booster sealed
7) Sealed two-starter decks (same clan)
8) Sealed two starter decks (different clan)
9) Standard Pre-Release Format
10) Storyline Tournament with a Limited (Draft) format
11) ...

This list is theoretically infinite. In which environment do you
balance the decks _more_? The answer is likely different for each
one.

I cast no aspersions on your intelligence, but I think we have a slang

translation of 'baited' for Henrik? Let me give you an example of
baited questioning.
When I was last in Germany, CNN International had a wonderful British
AM anchorman interviewing a representative of P & O Cruise Lines. One
of P&O's ships had recently suffered an outbreak of that nasty stomach
virus that has hit a number of cruise lines. Forty-some people were
affected. The rest (over 1100 passengers, IIRC) hardly knew about it,
until the ship turned around early to return to port, and contain the
problem. The 'interview' went something like this;

Anchor: How exactly is it that a company like P&O can think to
continue sentting sail with this obvious black mark on their company?
Representative: We consider one contained outbreak to be a serious
issue, but one that won't keep us from providing our fine service to
the cruise industry.

Anchor: When will you be reimbursing all of the cruise-goers from this
nightmare vacation gone awry for thier ruined holiday?
Rep: We will be dealing with customer complainsts on a case-by-case
basis, and responding fairly and appropriately.

Anchor: But all of those people paid a large sum for a cruise that put
their health in serious jeopardy, and then had it cut short by and
early return... I just want to know when it is that they will be
getting their money back?
Rep: We will be dealing with customer complainsts on a case-by-case
basis, and responding fairly and appropriately.

Yes, some questions are bad for a company to answer. In each case,
the Anchor's questions beg a greater level or atrocity than was really
present, and attempted to catch (hence, bait) the representative into
commiting his company to a course of action that would exceed what is
appropriate. In this instance, the representative was forced by
circumstance to respond to such questions, and did so by wisely not
answering them directly. Answering the above directly would be
suicidal, and the Anchor knows it. So does the Rep.

for the decks. Whats more, a fix to make the !Tor deck stronger will
likely leave some other deck (and its associated fans) as the weakest

by thousands, and that business model is doomed to failure.

Why not do so? Because no matter how much better you balance the
decks, there will always be a deck that is weakest (in certain
environments). The value of additional work diminishes exponentially,
so one has to draw a line somewhere as to how much work is done
balancing decks. The actual playability differences between all of
the starters (with the possible exception of the !Venture) is small.
Much smaller than this thread implies. Whats more, none of this takes
into account the format of the game, either. Given the right
circumstance (say, two-deck sealed with different clans), I'd be
picking up the !Tor as my main deck.

I playtested for a CCG with a small player base. CCG also happened to be power
rare heavy. We ran into a problem that I'm sure is run into often even if it
is usually a minor one and even if it's rarely noticed. The problem was that
we were playing on a different level than the average player. More
specifically, because we were playing on a different level, it became unclear
how to fix cards/strategies while playtesting. If we balanced for our level,
then it would appear unbalanced to the people who didn't have all of the
rares/ultrarares/promos and/or to the people who didn't understand the rules
(the original rulebook was crap, for instance, it lacked timing rules, which
weren't decided upon until the first expansion) and/or to the people who
thought they were a lot better than they were, a more common situation with a
smaller player base.

I don't think it's possible to try to have playtesters test to the level of
someone else because they wouldn't know when they are supposed to be "smart"
and when not. Of course, ideally, playtesters are 1) better than the masses
and 2) try to educate the masses to close the gap in knowledge and skill. In
practice, doesn't work so well.

precons. They really don't see much play as far as I can tell. Then, they
quickly morph when adding cards. One of the major reasons I think different
areas get different results at the prereleases is that they play them under
different rules. Some draft, some don't. Some play with more cards. Some
trade. Etc.

When we tested precons for that CCG, we didn't test adding any cards until the
second batch were in the works, course we had all of about 3 weeks to test the
original set's nonprecon cards, which was just great for producing a balanced
game (then, new rules got added into the rulebook after playtesting was over,
have I ranted lately about how playtesting was the most frustrating thing I've
ever done vis-a-vis CCGs?). The second batch never got made. Point being that
it's not likely to be a top priority to get precons to play right. I guess
another point might be that, even if it were a top priority, playing precons
